Cross-validation by refitting, leaving out whole individuals or groups

Source: R/loo-hazard.R
kfold_hazard.Rd

Estimates how well a model fitted with fit_hazard() predicts data it was not fitted to, by refitting it with each unit left out in turn and predicting the unit from the refit. It answers the same question as loo_hazard(), with the same choice of unit, but without its approximation: use it where loo_hazard() warns that PSIS cannot be trusted, which is typical when whole trials with a strong trial effect are left out.

Usage

kfold_hazard(fit, unit = NULL, K = NULL, ...)

Arguments

fit

A brmsfit, a model fitted with fit_hazard().

unit

An optional character string, the unit to leave out, as in loo_hazard().

K

An optional single whole number, the number of folds, from 2 to the number of units. NULL (the default) gives one fold per unit, leaving out each unit on its own.

...

Further arguments for the refits, passed to brms::brm() through stats::update(), such as chains, iter or cores.

Value

A kfold object in the layout of loo::kfold(), with one pointwise value per unit, which loo::loo_compare() accepts, and extra elements unit (its name), K, and folds (the fold of each unit).

Details

The units are split into K folds, and the model is refitted once per fold without that fold's units. A unit's rows are summed within each draw of the refit, so its value is its joint log predictive density, averaged over the draws. Where the unit's level of a group-level term was left out entirely (a whole trial), its effect is drawn from the fitted population distribution, so the trial is predicted as a new trial would be.

The refits take time: one model fit per fold. With K smaller than the number of units, the units are assigned to folds at random; call set.seed() first to get the same folds again. Models that are to be compared must be refitted with the same folds: with fewer folds than units, call set.seed() with the same seed before each call, or use fit_hazard_models(), which assigns the folds once for all the models.

The effect of a unit whose level was left out is drawn once for each draw of the refit, with R's own generator, and the unit's density is averaged over those draws. The average rests on the few draws whose effect lands near the unit's own, so the estimate varies from one run to the next: in three runs of one comparison of two models on eight trials, it moved by about 1 in elpd for each model (standard error about 18), as much as the two models differed. A seed gives the same estimate again, but does not make it more precise: set.seed() before the call fixes the folds and these draws, and so the estimate, on one computer. The refit keeps the priors of the fit it starts from, whose defaults are centred on the median failure temperature and time of all the data, the units left out included; they are weak, so this matters little, and it keeps the prior the same in every fold.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# a model fitted to a small ramping trial: 20 individuals warmed from 20 to 35
# degrees over 60 minutes and checked every minute, in two trials (see fit_hazard())
path   <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = c(0, 60), temp = c(20, 35))
checks <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = seq(0, 60, by = 1))
ind    <- data.frame(id = 1:20, path_id = "A", event = 1, mass = runif(20, 8, 12),
                     trial = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 10),
                     t_upper = sample(seq(10, 60, 10), 20, replace = TRUE))
long   <- build_hazard_data(ind, path, "interval", covariates = c("mass", "trial"),
                            checks = checks)

fit <- fit_hazard(long, "exp", dpar_formulas = list(loga = ~ 1 + (1 | trial)))
cv  <- kfold_hazard(fit, cores = 4)       # one refit per trial
} # }
